nameStory: The Black-horned Tree Cricket gets its name from the distinctive dark coloring on its antennae, which look like tiny black horns extending from its pale head. While most tree crickets have light-colored antennae, this species sports dramatically darker 'horns' that make identification much easier for nature enthusiasts.
description: The Black-horned Tree Cricket is a delicate, pale green to whitish insect about the size of your thumbnail. Like other tree crickets, it has a slender build with long, thread-like antennae and broad, translucent wings that it holds roof-like over its body. These musical insects are the chirping champions of late summer evenings, creating their songs by rubbing their wings together. Despite their name, they're found not just in trees but also in shrubs, tall grasses, and garden plants.

idTips.label: Dark Antennae
idTips.description: Look for distinctly blackened or dark brown antennae that contrast sharply with the pale body - this is the key feature that separates it from other tree crickets

idTips.label: Body Color
idTips.description: Pale green to creamy white body that feels smooth and delicate to the touch, often with a slightly translucent appearance

idTips.label: Wing Shape
idTips.description: Broad, clear wings held like a tent over the back when at rest, with visible veining that creates a lace-like pattern

idTips.label: Size and Build
idTips.description: Slender, delicate build about 12-15mm long with notably long, thin legs that feel fragile if gently handled

idTips.label: Evening Song
idTips.description: Produces a continuous, musical trill in warm evenings - softer and more melodious than the harsh chirping of ground crickets

habitat: Black-horned Tree Crickets thrive in New England's gardens, forest edges, and areas with mixed vegetation including both woody plants and tall grasses. They particularly favor raspberry and blackberry patches, fruit trees, and shrubby areas where they can easily move between different plant layers. You'll often find them in suburban gardens and along woodland borders where there's a good mix of trees, shrubs, and herbaceous plants.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active; eggs laid the previous fall are developing in plant stems and bark crevices.
seasonality.summer: Young nymphs begin appearing in early summer, growing through several molts. Adults become active in mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Peak activity period when adults are singing, mating, and laying eggs. This is the best time to hear their evening concerts and spot them on plants.
seasonality.winter: Adults die with the first hard frosts, leaving behind eggs that will overwinter in plant tissue until the following year.

funFact: Black-horned Tree Crickets are living thermometers - you can actually calculate the temperature by counting their chirps! Count the number of chirps in 13 seconds and add 40 to get the temperature in Fahrenheit, making them remarkably accurate natural weather instruments.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Snowy Tree Crickets, but remember 'black horns, black-horned' - if the antennae are dark, you've found your Black-horned Tree Cricket. Snowy Tree Crickets have pale, unmarked antennae that match their whitish bodies.
contextualKnowledge: Tree crickets belong to a different family than the familiar black ground crickets most people know. They're much more delicate, musical, and arboreal in their habits, representing a completely different lifestyle from their ground-dwelling cousins.
compareHints: Among New England's tree crickets, the Black-horned is the easiest to identify thanks to its dark antennae. The Snowy Tree Cricket is similar in size and color but has pale antennae, while the Narrow-winged Tree Cricket has distinctly narrower wings and different markings. The Four-spotted Tree Cricket has distinctive black spots on its antennae segments rather than the overall dark coloration of the Black-horned species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's tree crickets, this species stands out for its narrow wing shape compared to the broad-winged tree cricket's obviously wider wings.

Among New England's tree crickets, Pine Tree Cricket is unique in its exclusive preference for pine trees - Snowy Tree Crickets prefer deciduous trees and shrubs, while Broad-winged Tree Crickets favor fruit trees and berry bushes.

Among New England's tree crickets, the broad-winged species is distinguished by its wider male wings compared to the narrow-winged tree cricket, and its preference for deciduous trees rather than the pine-loving pine tree cricket.
Among New England's tree crickets, the snowy tree cricket has the palest, most translucent appearance.
Among New England's tree crickets, the Four-spotted is the only one with exactly four dark spots on its body.
